identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Ramanathaswamy Temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva and the southern site of the Char Dham circuit, and is also a Paadal Petra Sthalam hymned by the Nayanars. Temple tradition holds that Rama consecrated and worshipped a lingam here after the war in Lanka to expiate the sin of brahmahatya, with Sita fashioning a lingam from sand when Hanuman was delayed in bringing one from Kailasa. Pilgrims bathe at the 22 theerthams inside the temple precinct as a defining part of the visit.

governance.founderPatron: Expanded by the Pandyas in the 12th century; sanctum renovated with stone shipped from Trincomalee under the Jaffna king Jeyaveera Cinkaiariyan (1380-1410); the third corridor built under Muthuramalinga Setupati of Ramanathapuram (r. 1763-1795)
governance.managingAuthority: Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Nadu

narrative.documentedHistory:
The temple stands on Rameswaram island and occupies roughly 15 acres. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams glorified in the Tevaram hymns of the Nayanars, indicating worship at the site well before the surviving structures.

The Pandya dynasty expanded the temple during the twelfth century. The kings of Jaffna made substantial contributions: Jeyaveera Cinkaiariyan (1380-1410) is recorded as having shipped stone blocks from Trincomalee for the renovation of the sanctum. The Setupatis of Ramanathapuram were the temple's later patrons; Muthuramalinga Setupati (r. 1763-1795) built the third and outermost corridor for which the temple is best known.

The outer corridors stand about 6.9 m high and run roughly 400 ft east-west by 640 ft north-south, the inner corridors 224 ft by 352 ft; the combined corridor length is given as about 3,850 ft, with roughly 1,212 pillars in the outer corridor, each about 30 ft from floor to roof centre. The principal rajagopuram rises about 53 m.
narrative.sthalaPuranam: The HR&CE temple page records the traditional account that Rama, after the war in Lanka, consecrated and worshipped a Sivalinga here to expiate the sin of brahmahatya, and that when Hanuman was delayed in bringing a lingam from Mount Kailasa, Sita fashioned one from sand. The page also describes the island as shaped like a conch in the hands of Thirumal.

visitingInfo.entryRules: Bathing at the 22 theerthams inside the temple premises is permitted from 5:30 AM to 12:30 PM and from 3:00 PM to 7:00 PM.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Timings, theertham bathing hours and festival-day arrangements should be confirmed with the HR&CE temple office on 04573221223 or via rameswaramramanathar.hrce.tn.gov.in; the official page states its own opening hours inconsistently.

openingHours.notes: The HR&CE page is internally inconsistent: it gives a morning session of 4:00 AM to 1:00 PM while also stating that devotees are admitted from 5:00 AM. The later admission time is recorded here as the practical opening; verify before travelling.

The HR&CE page gives an afternoon/evening session of 3:00 PM to 8:00 PM but also states that the temple closes at 9:00 PM daily; the Ardhajama pooja is listed at 8:30 PM, consistent with the later closing. Verify before travelling.

poojas.description: The last pooja of the day.

shrines.locationDescription: The sanctum holds two lingams: the Ramalingam, which tradition says Rama made from sand, and the Vishvalingam, said to have been brought by Hanuman from Kailasa.
A separate shrine for the goddess within the complex.
A separate goddess shrine within the complex.
The outermost pillared corridor, built under Muthuramalinga Setupati (r. 1763-1795); about 6.9 m high, running roughly 400 ft east-west by 640 ft north-south, with about 1,212 pillars.

Twenty-two holy wells inside the temple premises, traditionally identified with the 22 arrows in Rama's quiver. Pilgrims bathe at them in sequence; bathing is permitted 5:30 AM to 12:30 PM and 3:00 PM to 7:00 PM. Agni Theertham, the shore of the Bay of Bengal immediately east of the temple, is counted with them.
The principal tower of the temple, about 53 m tall.
